B.h1("VI.  THE APPLICABLE STANDARD FOR EMERGENCY MEASURES")
B.para("Article 29(1) of the Rules permits a party “that needs urgent interim or conservatory measures that cannot await the constitution of an arbitral tribunal” to apply for such measures. Article 28(1) authorizes “any interim or conservatory measure [the tribunal] deems appropriate,” and Article 6(7) of Appendix V permits the emergency arbitrator to make the Order “subject to such conditions as the emergency arbitrator thinks appropriate, including requiring the provision of appropriate security.” The parties also agreed that the arbitrator “shall have the authority to award any remedy or relief that would be available from a court,” including equitable relief (EA § 12(a); IPA § 9.1), and that emergency measures may be granted to “preserve the status quo, prevent irreparable harm, or protect or preserve the subject matter of the dispute” (EA § 12(c)).")
B.para("Neither the Rules nor Appendix V prescribes a substantive test. Emergency arbitrators acting under the Rules have consistently considered, as reflected in the ICC Commission Report on Emergency Arbitrator Proceedings (2019), whether the applicant has shown: (1) prima facie jurisdiction; (2) urgency, in the sense that the measures cannot await the constitution of the tribunal; (3) a risk of irreparable or serious harm not adequately reparable by damages; (4) a reasonable possibility of success on the merits (a prima facie case), without prejudging the merits; and (5) proportionality, i.e., that the balance of convenience favours the measures.")
B.para("These criteria are consistent with the law of the seat and the governing law. Under New York law, a preliminary injunction requires a likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable injury absent relief, and a balance of equities in the movant’s favour (*Doe v. Axelrod*, 73 N.Y.2d 748, 750 (1988)); and a New York court may grant provisional relief in aid of arbitration where the award “may be rendered ineffectual without such provisional relief” (N.Y. C.P.L.R. 7502(c)). The Second Circuit applies materially the same test in trade-secret and restrictive-covenant cases (*Faiveley Transport Malmo AB v. Wabtec Corp.*, 559 F.3d 110, 116 (2d Cir. 2009); *Ticor Title Ins. Co. v. Cohen*, 173 F.3d 63, 68–69 (2d Cir. 1999)). Pinnacle invokes these authorities as persuasive guidance; the Emergency Arbitrator is not bound by domestic procedural standards for court injunctions.")

B.para("**Choice of law.** Pinnacle anticipates that Dr. Mehta, a Texas resident employed in Texas, may contend that Texas law governs the covenant notwithstanding the parties’ New York choice of law (EA § 12(b)). Texas likewise enforces non-competition covenants that are ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement — including an employer’s provision of confidential information — and reasonable as to time, geography and scope of activity (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 15.50–15.52; *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)), and Texas courts must reform rather than void an overbroad covenant (§ 15.51(c)). The covenant here was given in exchange for access to Pinnacle’s most sensitive Confidential Information (EA Recitals; § 7(d)(ii)). B.h3("7.  Breach of fiduciary duty")
B.para("As Pinnacle’s CTO through 9 May 2025, Dr. Mehta owed Pinnacle a duty of undivided loyalty and was contractually bound to “act in the best interests of the Company at all times” (EA § 2(d)). Systematically copying Pinnacle’s core technology to personal media while corresponding with a competitor’s CEO about “next steps” and “timing and logistics” is, prima facie, a breach of that duty (*cf. Phansalkar v. Andersen Weinroth & Co.*, 344 F.3d 184, 200–02 (2d Cir. 2003) (faithless-servant doctrine)). This claim reinforces the prima facie case but is not necessary to any measure sought.")

B.h2("D.  Pinnacle faces imminent, irreparable harm that damages cannot remedy")

B.para("**Loss of trade secrets.** “A trade secret once lost is, of course, lost forever,” and its loss “cannot be measured in money damages” (*FMC Corp. v. Taiwan Tainan Giant Indus. Co.*, 730 F.2d 61, 63 (2d Cir. 1984)). Irreparable harm is established where there is a danger that a misappropriator will disseminate the secrets more widely or otherwise irreparably impair their value (*Faiveley*, 559 F.3d at 118–19). Both dangers are present: the materials sit on an unaccounted-for USB device and in a personal cloud account susceptible to untraceable forwarding (Finding 6.3), and the person holding them now directs development of a competing product for a competitor that has publicly accelerated its launch. Once Zenith source code, schematics or customer specifications are incorporated into Helix or disclosed to Vortech personnel, no award can restore their secrecy.")

These consequences are inherently difficult to quantify and to reverse once the market has moved.")
B.para("**Inadequacy of damages.** Pinnacle’s CEO estimates Dr. Mehta’s personal net worth at approximately US$3.5 million (**C-8**, § V) — a fraction of Pinnacle’s exposure and of its US$37.2 million investment. A damages award against Dr. Mehta could not make Pinnacle whole.")

B.para("The measures impose minimal legitimate burden on Dr. Mehta. B.para("By contrast, refusing the measures would expose Pinnacle to the permanent loss of its most valuable technology, the erosion of a US$37.2 million investment and a projected first-mover position, and the potential loss of key personnel — harm the Respondent’s own agreement characterizes as irreparable.")
